how: Six studies comparing 2,159 people with lung cancer and 2,985 without were pooled. Regular cannabis smoking wasn't clearly linked to lung cancer, even in people who didn't smoke tobacco, but a higher risk couldn't be ruled out. We know this pooled study only from an expert committee's report.

A Swedish study followed 49,321 men for 40 years, from military call-up at 18 to 20 to about age 60. Men who said at call-up they'd used cannabis over 50 times got lung cancer about twice as often as men who said never. That held even allowing for the tobacco they smoked then.

But 91 in 100 of those men also smoked tobacco. The 678 men who used cannabis without tobacco had one lung cancer between them: too few to study cannabis alone. Among men who'd used it less, risk didn't clearly rise with more use, and nobody asked what anyone smoked later.

By about 60, 189 of the 49,321 men, about 4 in 1,000, had a lung cancer record; the paper doesn't say how many in each group. Lung cancer is usually found at about 70. An expert committee notes that cannabis smoke, like tobacco smoke, contains cancer-causing chemicals.

how: 17 healthy adults came to a lab six times. On average, they hadn't used cannabis for about a year. Each time they got the same weed, smoked in a small pipe or breathed in from a vaporizer, at a lower or higher amount, or a dummy.

At the lower amount, heart rate rose by 23 beats a minute after vaping against 11 after smoking, and people rated the effect about 70 out of 100 against 46. At the higher amount, neither gap was clear. Blood THC ran higher after vaping, but the study didn't test whether that was more than chance.

Where the two ways differed on attention and speed tasks, all three gaps showed worse scores after vaping. At the higher amount, both raised ratings of bad feelings, anxiety, memory trouble and coughing, with no clear gap. There was one case of vomiting after each way and one of hallucinations after vaping, all at the higher amount: too few to compare.

After the higher amount, people still rated an effect when their blood THC was back to zero. The study didn't test joints, bongs, handheld vapes, oil carts, concentrates, regular use, or effects on the lungs.

how: To count, a person had vaped or dabbed in the past 90 days, had changes in the lungs on a scan, and had no other likely cause. Half were 24 or younger, and 66 in 100 were male. CDC figures quoted second-hand: 52 deaths by mid-December 2019, about 2 in 100 cases, and in an earlier count 47 in 100 needed intensive care.

Of 2,022 patients who said what they'd vaped in the 3 months before, 82 in 100 named a THC product and 14 in 100 only nicotine. Nobody checked their devices, and in one study THC turned up in the lungs of 9 of 11 patients who said they hadn't used it.

Vitamin E acetate, a form of vitamin E sold online to cut or thicken cannabis oil, was in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients and none of 99 healthy people, who didn't vape THC. It was in 23 of 36 cartridge liquids from 10 New York patients. The papers call those cartridges illegal or fake, without saying how they knew.

None of this proves it caused the injury: the healthy people didn't vape THC, and nobody tested people who vaped the same products and stayed well, or what breathing it in does. The CDC says other chemicals aren't ruled out. Weed smoked, eaten or vaped as dried flower wasn't studied.
